demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Maladaptive Strategies.value: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events

Threat.value: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think

Memory.value: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

Negative Appraisals.value: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: For an index trauma of unexpected/traumatic death of a loved one, 'betrayal by someone I trusted' is a poor fit unless the death involved clear interpersonal wrongdoing by a trusted person; nothing else in the profile supports that specific circumstance, so this item is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: 'Need to stay alert' at bedtime implies ongoing external danger, which is less coherent with bereavement-related trauma in the absence of any triggers or appraisals about current interpersonal/physical threat. The rest of the profile centers on loss, self-blame, fragmented reliving memory, and catastrophic interpretations of delay, making this item stand out as mismatched.

vignette:
Ama was 23 and early in her first full-time role as an environmental scientist when her older brother died unexpectedly. He had been driving home after a late shift, and when he stopped replying to her texts she told herself he was busy or his phone had died. Hours later, after a delay that stretched far beyond what felt normal, she got the call telling her there had been a crash and that he had not survived. What stayed with her was not a clear, tellable story but a set of jagged fragments: staring at her phone, the unbearable waiting, her mother’s voice breaking, the sense that the world had split before she could understand what was happening. Since then, whenever anything takes longer than expected, her whole body jolts before she can think. If a colleague is late back from field sampling or a family member does not answer right away, she is immediately certain something terrible is unfolding.

In the weeks after his death, Ama kept circling the same conclusions. She had come to believe that somebody else would have stopped it, and that if she had been a better sister, sharper, more responsible, somehow she would have done something too. She was certain the death said something shameful about the sort of person she was, someone who missed signs and failed the people she loved. She also could not get past how deeply unfair it felt that he was gone and nothing could undo it. Those beliefs pulled her into hours of self-blame, replaying what she had texted, when she had texted, whether she should have called sooner, and whether a different person would have acted decisively enough to change the outcome.

The memory itself was difficult for her to hold in one piece. When she tried to describe the night, she often stopped, saying she knew what happened but could not find words. At other moments she began to approach it and then mentally shoved it away before she could fully recall it. Yet the memory did not stay distant; it would seize her as if it were happening now, especially in moments of waiting. A delayed email, a missed call, brake lights massed on the highway during her commute to a wetlands site could suddenly make the original dread feel present rather than past. Because those fragments came with such force, she increasingly avoided television, films, or news stories involving accidents or sudden deaths, fearing they would pull her straight back into that night.

At work, where field schedules changed and teams often ran late returning from site visits, the pattern tightened. If a truck was delayed in traffic or a coworker’s location update did not come through on time, Ama’s chest would clench and her heart would race before she had formed a thought. She was sleeping badly, lying awake scanning for signs that something else was about to go wrong. In that exhausted, keyed-up state, she found herself starting arguments with her mother or friends over minor things, later recognizing that the conflict gave her somewhere to put the fear and agitation. The constant sense of danger also pushed her back into self-blame: if she was this alert now, she thought, maybe she should have been this alert then; maybe her brother died because she had been the kind of person who let herself be reassured.

Over time, the ways she tried to manage it seemed to make the whole experience harder to bear. The more she ruminated about what she should have done, the more fixed her conclusions became that another person would have coped better and that there was something fundamentally wrong with her. Picking arguments left her ashamed afterward, which she folded into the same harsh view of her character. Avoiding media and cutting off the memory before it fully unfolded meant the night remained as disconnected flashes that still hit her with full force, impossible to place firmly in the past. Because it never felt fully processed, each fresh surge of alarm seemed to confirm that the danger was still close and unresolved.

By the time she sought help, Ama was frightened by how small her life had become. She dreaded routine delays in the field and checked her phone compulsively whenever anyone was late. She was worn down by broken sleep and by the way ordinary waiting could turn, in an instant, into certainty that death was about to happen again. What finally brought her in was an argument at work after a routine scheduling change left her shaking in the bathroom, unable to explain why she felt as if she had been dropped back into the night her brother died. She said she wanted, more than anything, to remember him without feeling ambushed by the moment of losing him, but she was afraid that if she stopped blaming herself, she would be letting his death matter less.
